To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
extreme scorers of self-reported emotional eaters eat more after a sad movie or a stressful task than non-extreme scorers.
self-reported emotional eating scores significantly moderated the relation of distress to food intake in the extreme scorers but not in the entire sample.
self-reported emotional eating moderates the relation between distress-induced eating and negative mood and stress in extreme scorers, but not in low and medium scorers.

the question of whether self-report questionnaires can predict actual food intake.
the role of self-reported emotional hunger in the relation between negative mood and actual food intake.
the relation between stress, self-reported emotional eating and actual eating.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the relation between distress (e.g. sadness or stress) and actual food intake is moderated by self-reported emotional eating scores, but only in the extreme groups of emotional eaters (low or high emotional eaters).

self-reported emotional eating scores do moderate the relation between distress (e.g., sadness) and actual food intake, but that the effect of self-reported eating scores is not large enough to be detectable when using median splits or when the range of scores is not sufficiently large.
self-reported emotional eating is a valid predictor of food intake in response to distress, provided that the participants with the extreme scores are selected.

self-reported emotional eating is a promising tool for the prediction of distress-induced eating.
